title: Burst Accordion: latency vs cost annotated draft
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft that experiments with an "accordion" metaphor for summarizing burst behavior: how short, tall bursts (spikes) versus long, shallow surges (stretches) trade off tail latency and $/QPS under different runtime knobs. Goal is to produce a lightweight collateral piece we can share with SRE/product when discussing customer burst SLAs and pricing guidance.

High level finding (preview):
- Short, high-amplitude bursts drive p99 inflation disproportionately relative to cost; aggressive pre-warm or slotized capacity reduces p99 but increases idle cost.
- Long-duration modest increases in concurrency improve amortization and reduce $/query but expose p90 uplift when KV cache hit-rate collapses.
- There is a sweet spot (accordion fold level 2) where modest reserved capacity + opportunistic multiplexing cuts cost ~18% vs pure on-demand with p95 change <5%.

Methodology:
- Model: open-llama-13B-equivalent (fp16 runtime profile), typical chat workload 32 tokens prompt / 64 tokens output.
- Hardware: A100-40GB equivalent pools and mixed smaller-GPU pool for comparison.
- Workloads: three synthetic shapes run against our devbed:
  * Spike: 20s high peak @ 250 QPS, base 5 QPS
  * Stretch: 15m @ 40 QPS from base 5 QPS (ramp 30s)
  * Plateau: sustained 1h @ 20 QPS
- Knobs tested: pre-warm slots (#slots reserved), smallbatch static (batch=8), dynamic multiplexing (max-multi=32), KV-prefetch on/off.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms), steady-state QPS served, cost approximated from GPU-minute + amortized slot idle.

Raw numeric summary (single-run snapshot):
Columns: workload | knob | p50 | p90 | p95 | p99 | $/kQ (approx)
Spike | on-demand | 42ms | 210ms | 410ms | 1100ms | $9.8
Spike | reserved-4slots | 45ms | 95ms | 150ms | 260ms | $12.6
Spike | prefetch-on | 44ms | 85ms | 140ms | 240ms | $12.9

Stretch | on-demand | 48ms | 120ms | 200ms | 520ms | $7.5
Stretch | reserved-2slots | 50ms | 105ms | 160ms | 300ms | $8.9
Stretch | multiplex-max32 | 70ms | 150ms | 230ms | 410ms | $6.1

Plateau | on-demand | 40ms | 90ms | 120ms | 190ms | $6.8
Plateau | best-effort-tiling | 44ms | 95ms | 125ms | 210ms | $5.9

Interpretation notes (quick):
- For Spike: reserved slots dramatically compress tail latency (p99 down ~4x) at the cost of higher $/kQ because of idle time during base traffic. Prefetch helps but only when burst contains repeat prefixes; otherwise gains vanish.
- For Stretch: multiplexing reduces $/kQ a lot (shared batching) but pushes p50/p90 up compared to reserved slots. If customer tolerates slightly higher p90 (e.g., web UI non-blocking), it's attractive.
- For Plateau: steady-state is where tiling/packing and smallbatch optimizations shine; cost per Q declines and latencies are tight.

Accordion visualization (text):
Legend: each row shows relative tail inflation (bars) and cost delta vs baseline (numbers).
Spike: [||||||||||----] tail-heavy | +28% $/kQ
Stretch: [|||||-----] mid-tail | -18% $/kQ with multiplexing
Plateau: [|||-------] low-tail | -13% $/kQ with tiling

Ascii sparkline of p99 vs time for Spike (sample):
T0      T5s    T10s   T15s   T20s  T25s
p99:    1200   1150   1100   300    160   130
(brief note: steep drop after burst due to slot cool-down)

Tradeoffs matrix (text bullets):
- Reserved slots: best tail, predictable, cost premium during low base traffic. Good for enterprise UI where p99 SLA matters.
- Multiplexing: best $/Q for sustained mid-level bursts, introduces p50/p90 variability. Good for batch/async workloads.
- Prefetch/KV: huge wins when workload repeats tokens across sessions (search/chat assistants with shared prompts). Marginal otherwise.
- Smallbatch vs largebatch: smallbatch reduces p99 but hurts throughput; largebatch better for throughput-night windows.

Operational checklist (for a customer-facing brief):
1) Capture burst type: duration and amplitude (we should add a short survey template).
2) Recommend default "accordion fold" per burst profile: fold 0 (no reserve) / fold1 (2 slots) / fold2 (4 slots) / fold3 (8+).
3) Provide an example cost estimate table per fold and expected p95/p99 bounds.
4) Add a short explainer on KV hit-rate sensitivity (how cache TTL and session affinity change outcomes).

Example customer snippet (two-sentence):
- "If your product sees short, sharp spikes (login waves, promo drops) we recommend fold2 reserved slots to protect p99; this raises baseline cost by ~25% but keeps tail within interactive bounds. For sustained higher concurrency (>20 QPS) prefer multiplexing + tiling to cut unit cost."

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need systematic measurement of KV-hit-rate distributions across real customer traces (ask observability for 90-day sample).
- Validate results on smaller GPUs (V100/T4) for multi-tenant economics.
- Flesh out price impact model: include provisioning discounts, preemptible usage, and GPU amortization curve.
- Decide canonical fold definitions (what exactly is fold2?).

Appendix (quick methods & run ids):
- Devbed run ids: run-29B-20290501A (Spike), run-29B-20290501B (Stretch). Raw traces stored in S3 bucket s3://redwood-devbench/burst-accordion/ (internal).
- Command flags: --dyn-mux=32 --reserve-slots=4 --kv-prefetch=true --batching=small

Notes to self: keep language customer-facing but retain enough numbers to be actionable. Turn this into a one-pager for Solutions Eng and an internal slide (2 slides) comparing fold2 vs multiplex baseline.

Contacts: Jonah for run reproducibility, Elena for graphs, Ravi for cost model input.

End of draft.
